questions.q: A writer reconstructs a scene she didn't witness from careful interviews with everyone present. Does this break Hersey's rule?
choices: Yes: any scene not witnessed is invention
Only if it's in the present tense
Only if it's in a newspaper
No: reconstruction from evidence is reporting; invention is what's forbidden
questions.explain: Hersey's own Hiroshima reconstructs scenes from interviews.

questions.q: What is Malcolm's central charge against journalists?
choices: They win subjects' trust to get material, then write the story they see, which the subject never agreed to
questions.explain: She treats this betrayal as built into the job, using the McGinniss–MacDonald case.

questions.q: Which practice does mainstream journalism treat as unacceptable without disclosure, and often outright?
questions.explain: Combining several people into one figure misleads readers about who exists.

choices: The unstated agreement about what a form promises about accuracy
The legal agreement between writer and publisher
The nut graf's promise of what the story is about
questions.explain: News, memoir and 'based on a true story' each promise different things. Ethical failures breach the promise.

questions.q: A writer merges three conversations held over a week into one scene. What's the minimum ethical step?
choices: Disclose it, for example in an author's note
questions.explain: Compression is contested; disclosure lets readers adjust their trust.

questions.q: Which criticism is commonly made of Malcolm's argument?
choices: Her opening generalizes too sweepingly; reporters can be honest with subjects about what they're doing
questions.explain: Many journalists accept her point about the relationship but reject its absolute verdict.

questions.q: Why do fabrication scandals, such as Janet Cooke's in 1981, damage more than one story?
choices: They make readers suspicious of every vivid true story
They only affect the writer involved
questions.explain: Narrative journalism depends on trust that nothing was invented.

ideas: A novelist may borrow from reality, but a journalist may not borrow from imagination.
The relationship between a journalist and a subject is built on a trust the finished story usually betrays.
Readers of each form carry an unstated contract about accuracy, and changes they aren't told about breach it.
